pos: n. (a stone of proverbial hardness; used figuratively of a set forehead and of a set heart)
etymology: Greek adamas, unconquerable, from a-, not, and damao, to subdue — that which cannot be broken. The Hebrew shamiyr names a stone harder than flint, used to cut and to engrave.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice, and the two uses are opposites that share a single property. God says to Ezekiel, sent to a people who would not hear: “As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house” (Eze 3:9). The prophet is given a hardness he did not have — not in the heart, which was to remain tender enough to sit astonished seven days among the captives, but in the forehead, the face that must not flinch when the house looks at him. Zechariah then uses the same stone for the sin: “they made their hearts as an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the LORD of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the LORD of hosts” (Zec 7:12). Both are unbreakable; one is a gift and one is a judgment. The distinction is the whole doctrine of a faithful ministry: God hardens the servant's face against fear of men, and men harden their own hearts against the word. Notice also who does the making. God says, I have made thy forehead; of the hearts Zechariah says, they made their hearts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines adamant as a very hard or impenetrable stone; a name given to the diamond and other substances of extreme hardness; used figuratively for impenetrable hardness.
webster_full: ADAMANT, n. A very hard or impenetrable stone; a name given to the diamond and other substances of extreme hardness.
2. Figuratively, anything of impenetrable hardness.
They made their hearts as an adamant stone. Zech. vii.
scriptures: Eze 3:9
As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house.
Zec 7:12

Yea, they made their hearts as an adamant stone, lest they should hear the law, and the words which the LORD of hosts hath sent in his spirit by the former prophets: therefore came a great wrath from the LORD of hosts.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: Hardness of heart is now diagnosed as an injury a person has sustained rather than a thing a person has done, and Zechariah 7:12 says plainly that they made their hearts so.
corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah's grammar is the point of the verse. They made their hearts as an adamant stone — not, their hearts became hard, and certainly not, their hearts were hardened by what was done to them. The chapter says what they refused: they refused to hearken, and pulled away the shoulder, and stopped their ears that they should not hear. Hardening is presented as a series of choices, each one small, ending in a condition no argument can penetrate. The modern account of the same phenomenon is almost entirely passive. A hard man is understood to be a wounded man, his hardness a defensive formation produced by what he has suffered, and the remedy accordingly therapeutic. Scripture does not deny that suffering is real or that it presses on the soul — Ezekiel sat astonished among the captives by the river Chebar for seven days. But it locates the hardening in the will, which is why it can be repented of and why it is judged. Two mercies follow from that. The first is that a man is not the helpless product of his history. The second is greater: the only cure for an adamant heart is not softening but replacement, and God promises exactly that — I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. That is regeneration, and it is a work God does, not one a man performs on himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamiyr (H8068), a hard stone, diamond, adamant, also a brier; chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to harden; qashah (H7185), to be hard or stiff-necked.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamiyr (H8068) — a hard sharp stone, adamant; used of Ezekiel's forehead, of the hardened heart, and of a pen of iron with the point of a diamond; Ezekiel 3:9, Zechariah 7:12, Jeremiah 17:1.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to make firm, to harden; the verb of Pharaoh's heart and of the strengthened prophet; Exodus 7:13, Ezekiel 3:8.
Hebrew qashah (H7185) — to be hard, severe, stiff; harden not your heart, as in the provocation; Psalm 95:8, Hebrews 3:8.
usage: “As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead” — hardness given to the servant, against fear.
“They made their hearts as an adamant stone” — hardness made by the man, against the word.
“I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh” — the only cure, and it is replacement.

pos: n. (a precious substance of Havilah, named with gold and onyx; also the standard of comparison for the colour of the manna)
etymology: Greek bdellion, from a Semitic root; either an aromatic gum-resin of pale waxy colour or a precious stone. The Authorized Version transliterates the Hebrew bedolach rather than guessing.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice and each time in a place of wonder. Genesis, describing the land the river Pison compasseth: “the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone” (Gen 2:12). Moses names three treasures of the unfallen world, and the naming is deliberate — Eden was not a bare garden but a place of good gold, precious gum, and stones, and the same materials reappear at the end of the Bible in the city whose foundations are garnished with all manner of precious stones. Then in the wilderness: “the manna was as coriander seed, and the colour thereof as the colour of bdellium” (Num 11:7), given in the middle of the people's complaint that they had nothing at all besides this manna. Bread came down from heaven six mornings a week for forty years, pale and translucent as a precious substance, and Israel called it light bread and remembered the fish of Egypt, which they did eat freely, and the cucumbers, and the melons. Christ takes the whole scene up in John 6 and applies it to Himself: I am that bread of life. Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bdellium as a gummy resinous juice produced by a tree in the East Indies and Arabia, of a bitter taste, and interpreted by some as a precious stone or pearl.
webster_full: BDELLIUM, n. A gummy resinous juice, produced by a tree in the East Indies, Arabia and Media; brought in pieces of the size of an olive, of a yellowish color.
2. The word in Scripture has been variously interpreted; some understanding a gum, others a precious stone, or pearl.
The colour thereof as the colour of bdellium. Num. xi.
scriptures: Gen 2:12
And the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone.
Num 11:6
But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.
Joh 6:49
Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.
corruption_summary: Familiar mercy is the mercy most despised: the same bread God likened to a precious substance was called nothing at all by the people who ate it every morning.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The identity of bdellium is genuinely uncertain and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise. The principle to recover is in the contrast between the narrator's description and the people's. The Holy Ghost describes the manna as coriander seed in shape and bdellium in colour — a precious thing, one of the three treasures of Eden used as the comparison. The congregation, eating it daily, said: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes. Nothing at all. Bread from heaven, gathered every morning without ploughing or sowing, and it had become invisible by being reliable. That is the ordinary fate of every constant mercy. Daily bread, a sound body, a household, the Scriptures in one's own language, the Lord's Day coming round again — the mercies most steadily given are the ones least noticed and most quickly complained about. Numbers 11 shows where the complaint went: they wept, and asked for flesh, and God gave them quails and sent leanness into their soul. The remedy Scripture prescribes is not more mercies but remembrance and thanksgiving — bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits — and the manna itself was preserved in a golden pot before the testimony for exactly that reason.
roots_summary: Hebrew bedolach (H916), bdellium; shoham (H7718), onyx; man (H4478), manna, from the question man hu, what is it?
roots_lines: Hebrew bedolach (H916) — bdellium; a gum-resin or a precious stone, named among the treasures of Havilah and used for the colour of the manna; Genesis 2:12, Numbers 11:7.
Hebrew shoham (H7718) — onyx; from Eden's river country to the shoulderpieces of the ephod and the high priest's breastplate; Genesis 2:12, Exodus 28:9.
Hebrew man (H4478) — manna; the name is the question the people asked, man hu, what is it? for they wist not what it was; Exodus 16:15, 16:31.
usage: “There is bdellium and the onyx stone” — the treasures of the unfallen world named in Genesis 2.
“The colour thereof as the colour of bdellium” — heaven's description of the bread.
“There is nothing at all, beside this manna” — the congregation's description of the same bread.

pos: n. (small stones and coarse sand; in Scripture, a figure of grit in the mouth and of innumerable multitude)
etymology: Old French gravele, coarse sand. The Authorized Version uses it for two Hebrew ideas: the grit that breaks the teeth, and the shingle of the shore that cannot be numbered.
biblical_def: Solomon gives the proverb: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel” (Pro 20:17). Dishonest gain has a taste and a sequel, and the sequel is grit — the mouth that enjoyed the bread grinding stones. Isaiah takes the other sense in a lament over what might have been: “Thy seed also had been as the sand, and the offspring of thy bowels like the gravel thereof; his name should not have been cut off nor destroyed from before me” (Isa 48:19), the verse immediately after O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river. Disobedience cost a multitude. Jeremiah then puts the first image into the mouth of a suffering man: “He hath also broken my teeth with gravel stones, he hath covered me with ashes” (Lam 3:16) — the prophet in the middle of the great acrostic lament, ascribing his affliction directly to God. Twenty verses later in the same chapter comes This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is the same speaker. The Bible allows a man to say both things, in that order, without correcting the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gravel as small stones or fragments of stone, or very small pebbles, larger than the particles of sand, but often intermixed with them.
webster_full: GRAVEL, n. Small stones or fragments of stone, or very small pebbles, larger than the particles of sand, but often intermixed with them.
2. In medicine, small calculous concretions in the kidneys and bladder.
GRAVEL, v.t. To cover with gravel; to puzzle or embarrass.
scriptures: Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.
Thy seed also had been as the sand, and the offspring of thy bowels like the gravel thereof; his name should not have been cut off nor destroyed from before me.
Lam 3:16
He hath also broken my teeth with gravel stones, he hath covered me with ashes.
corruption_summary: Lamentations 3 is quoted from verse 22 onward and almost never from verse 16, so that the church has the comfort of the chapter without the honesty that earns it.
corruption_paragraphs: Lamentations 3:22-23 is one of the best-loved passages in the Old Testament — it is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. It is sung, printed, and cross-stitched. Verse 16 is from the same speaker, six verses earlier: he hath broken my teeth with gravel stones, he hath covered me with ashes. So are verses 1 to 18, which say that God has led him into darkness, made his chain heavy, shut out his prayer, bent His bow and set him as a mark for the arrow, and that his strength and his hope are perished from the LORD. Scripture prints the whole thing. The comfort of verse 22 is not a correction of verse 16 and not an alternative perspective on it; it is the same man, in the same affliction, recalling something to mind. A Christianity that keeps only the second half teaches its people that faith means never saying the first half, and so leaves them speechless in the very hour Lamentations was given for. The Psalter is largely lament. Job argues for thirty-five chapters. The Man of sorrows cried, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? The hope in verse 24 — the LORD is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him — is worth having precisely because the man saying it has told the truth about the gravel.
roots_summary: Hebrew chatsats (H2687), gravel, grit; me'ah, the shingle of the shore in Isaiah's figure; chowl (H2344), sand, the standard of innumerable multitude.
roots_lines: Hebrew chatsats (H2687) — gravel, grit, small stones; the mouth filled with it after the bread of deceit, and the broken teeth of Lamentations; Proverbs 20:17, Lamentations 3:16.
Hebrew chowl (H2344) — sand; the covenant figure for a countless seed, promised to Abraham and mourned by Isaiah; Genesis 22:17, Isaiah 48:19.
Hebrew 'epher (H665) — ashes; the covering of mourning and repentance; Lamentations 3:16, Job 42:6.
usage: “Bread of deceit is sweet…but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel” — the taste and the sequel.
“The offspring of thy bowels like the gravel thereof” — the multitude disobedience cost.
“He hath broken my teeth with gravel stones” — verse 16 of the chapter we quote from verse 22.

pos: n. pl. (thick boards of timber; in the temple, the fir flooring and the thick boards of the porch)
etymology: Old French planche, a board. Distinguished in the Authorized Version from boards, which are lighter, and from beams, which carry weight.
biblical_def: Solomon “built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir” (1Ki 6:15). Cedar on the walls, fir underfoot — and not one stone of the costly masonry left showing inside. The next verses say the cedar was carved with knops and open flowers, and that the whole house was overlaid with gold; the account is careful to add that there was no stone seen. In Ezekiel's visionary temple the planks return: “there were thick planks upon the face of the porch without” (Eze 41:25), and again with the narrow windows and the palm trees on the sides of the porch (Eze 41:26). Two chapters of a book written to exiles are given to measurements of a house they could not see, and the reason is stated at the end: shew the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern. God gives a precise design to a homeless people as a summons to holiness. Planks are humble things, and Scripture records them because the house of God is built out of humble things exactly specified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a plank as a broad piece of sawed timber, differing from a board only in being thicker; and figuratively, that on which one stands or relies.
webster_full: PLANK, n. A broad piece of sawed timber, differing from a board only in being thicker.
2. In seamen's language, planks are the thick boards with which a ship's side and deck are covered.
PLANK, v.t. To cover or lay with planks.
scriptures: And he built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir.
And there were made on them, on the doors of the temple, cherubims and palm trees, like as were made upon the walls; and there were thick planks upon the face of the porch without.
All this, said David, the LORD made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern.
corruption_summary: The building chapters are skipped as tedious inventory, and with them goes the doctrine they exist to teach: that God specifies how He is to be approached and does not leave it to the builder's taste.
corruption_paragraphs: Whole chapters of Exodus, 1 Kings, and Ezekiel consist of measurements, materials, and joinery, and they are among the least-read pages in the Bible. The reason they are there is doctrinal, not decorative. David says of the temple plan, All this the LORD made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern (1Ch 28:19); Moses was warned of God when he was about to make the tabernacle, See that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount (Heb 8:5). The house in which God is approached is designed by God, down to the planks of fir on the floor. That principle survives the ceremonial law and appears in the New Testament as the regulative principle of worship, which the 1689 Confession states plainly: the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by Himself, and so limited by His own revealed will, that He may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scriptures. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire and died for it; Uzzah steadied the ark with the best of intentions. Modern worship planning is very largely a discussion of taste, effect, and audience. The building chapters, tedious as they look, are the standing reminder that God has always told His people exactly how He would be approached.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsela' (H6763), a side, a board or plank; 'ets (H6086), wood, timber; berowsh (H1265), fir or cypress, the wood of the temple floor.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsela' (H6763) — a rib, a side, a plank or board; used of the boards of the temple and of the rib taken from Adam; 1 Kings 6:15, Genesis 2:22.
Hebrew berowsh (H1265) — fir or cypress; the flooring of Solomon's house and the timber Hiram sent from Lebanon; 1 Kings 6:15, 1 Kings 5:8.
Hebrew tabniyth (H8403) — a pattern, a model; the plan shewed to Moses in the mount and given to David in writing; Exodus 25:9, 1 Chronicles 28:19.
usage: “Covered the floor of the house with planks of fir” — and there was no stone seen.
“Thick planks upon the face of the porch without” — a design given to exiles who could not build it.
“All the works of this pattern” — the house of God is not left to the builder's taste.

pos: n. pl. (the beams on which wheels turn; in Solomon's temple, part of the ten brasen bases that carried the lavers)
etymology: Middle English axeltre, from Old Norse oxull, an axis, and tree in the older sense of a beam of wood. The temple axletrees were molten brass, not timber.
biblical_def: Hiram of Tyre cast ten brasen bases for the ten lavers of Solomon's temple, and the account is minute: “under the borders were four wheels; and the axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base: and the height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit” (1Ki 7:32); “the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten” (1Ki 7:33). Everything in that sentence is a wheelwright's word — axletree, nave, felloe, spoke — and every part was cast solid in brass. The lavers were for washing that which they offered for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in. The point of the wheels was mobility: the water of cleansing was made to be brought where the work was, rather than the work carried to the water. A temple could have been built with fixed basins; this one was built with chariot wheels under them. Ezekiel later sees wheels of another order beside the living creatures, with rings full of eyes, and the spirit of the living creature in the wheels — and the God who cast the little brasen wheels rides the great ones.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an axletree as a piece of timber or bar of iron, fitted for insertion in the hobs or naves of wheels, on which the wheels turn.
webster_full: AXLETREE, n. A piece of timber or bar of iron, fitted for insertion in the hobs or naves of wheels, on which the wheels turn.
NAVE, n. The thick piece of timber in the middle of a wheel, in which the spokes are inserted.
FELLOE, n. The exterior part of a wheel, composed of pieces of timber joined to the spokes.
scriptures: And under the borders were four wheels; and the axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base: and the height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit.
And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten.

He made also ten lavers, and put five on the right hand, and five on the left, to wash in them: such things as they offered for the burnt offering they washed in them; but the sea was for the priests to wash in.
corruption_summary: Cleansing is treated as something the sinner must travel to and qualify for, when the temple's own furniture was built on wheels to be brought to the place of the work.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. An axletree is an axletree. The detail worth preaching is that God had the lavers mounted on chariot wheels. The great brasen sea stood fixed on twelve oxen, and the priests washed there; but the ten lavers, in which the parts of the burnt offering were rinsed, could be rolled to wherever the butchering and the burning were happening. The water went to the work. That is a small mechanical fact with a large pastoral shape, because the persistent instinct of religion is the reverse — that a man must clean himself up and travel to the place of cleansing under his own power, arriving presentable. Scripture's picture is of a God who comes: to the garden calling Adam, to Egypt to bring out a nation, to a manger, to a Samaritan woman at a well at noon, to Zacchaeus in a tree, to Saul on the Damascus road. Titus 3:5 states the doctrine — not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost. The wheels under the lavers were cast solid in brass, naves, felloes, spokes and all, because a thing that must move where the work is has to be made strong.
roots_summary: Hebrew yad (H3027), a hand, and so an axle or support; 'owphan (H212), a wheel; kiyowr (H3595), a laver or basin.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'owphan (H212) — a wheel; the wheels of the brasen bases, and the wheels of Ezekiel's vision beside the living creatures; 1 Kings 7:32, Ezekiel 1:15.
Hebrew kiyowr (H3595) — a laver, a basin; the ten wheeled lavers of the temple and the laver of brass at the tabernacle door; 1 Kings 7:38, Exodus 30:18.
Hebrew chishshuq / chishshur — the spokes and naves of the wheel; the wheelwright's vocabulary carried over into cast brass; 1 Kings 7:33.
usage: “The axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base” — the lavers built to be moved.
“Their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten” — a chariot wheel cast in brass.
“Such things as they offered for the burnt offering they washed in them” — the water brought to the work.

pos: n. pl. (garments worn in front of the body; in Genesis, the fig-leaf coverings of the first sin)
etymology: Middle English napron, from Old French naperon, a small cloth; the n migrated to the article. The Hebrew chagorah is a girdle or loincloth — a covering only of the middle.
biblical_def: “The eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons” (Gen 3:7). The first act of fallen man was a covering of his own manufacture, and Scripture records its dimensions exactly: it was a girdle, a covering of the middle only, made of leaves that would wither by evening, and it did not work — a few verses later Adam is still saying, I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself. God's answer stands at the end of the chapter: unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them. Coats, not girdles; skin, not leaf; made by God, not by the man; and something died to provide them. That is the first blood shed in the Bible and the first picture of substitution. The word appears once more, at Ephesus, where God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul, “so that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them” (Act 19:12) — the workman's apron of a tentmaker, used of God in a city famous for its magic, until they which used curious arts brought their books together and burned them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apron as a cloth or piece of leather worn on the fore part of the body, to keep the clothes clean or defend them from injury.
webster_full: APRON, n. A cloth or piece of leather worn on the fore part of the body, to keep the clothes clean, or defend them from injury.
2. The fat skin covering the belly of a goose or duck.
3. A piece of lead which covers the touch-hole of a cannon.
scriptures: Gen 3:7
And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.
Gen 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.
corruption_summary: Every religion of human effort is a fig-leaf apron: a covering the sinner sews himself, sized to hide only what embarrasses him, out of material that will not last the day.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 3:7 and 3:21 stand fourteen verses apart and between them lies the whole difference between religion and the gospel. Man's covering: fig leaves, sewn by the guilty, covering the middle, dead by morning, and demonstrably useless — Adam wearing his apron still hid among the trees. God's covering: coats of skins, made by the LORD God, covering the whole body, and costing the life of an animal. The pattern set there governs the rest of the Bible. Isaiah's filthy rags are fig leaves; the Pharisee's tithe of mint and anise and cummin is a fig leaf; the indulgence, the pilgrimage, the treasury of merit, the sincere effort to be a good person, the modern self-justification by cause and identity — all of them are aprons, and they share the three marks: self-made, partial, and perishable. The gospel answer is not an improved apron. It is Christ, of whom Paul says, as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ, and of whom Isaiah says, he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness. And a death provided it, as a death provided the skins. The one thing a man cannot do with the righteousness of Christ is sew it himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew chagorah (H2290), a girdle, a loincloth; kethoneth (H3801), a coat or tunic covering the body; Greek simikinthion (G4612), a workman's apron.
roots_lines: Hebrew chagorah (H2290) — a girdle or apron, a covering of the loins only; the fig-leaf garment of Genesis 3:7.
Hebrew kethoneth (H3801) — a coat, a tunic; God's covering of skins, and the same word as Joseph's coat of many colours and the priest's holy coat; Genesis 3:21, 37:3, Exodus 28:4.
Greek simikinthion (G4612) — a narrow apron worn by workmen; used once, of the cloths carried from Paul's body at Ephesus; Acts 19:12.
usage: “They sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons” — the first religion of human manufacture.
“The LORD God make coats of skins, and clothe them” — the first blood, and the first substitution.
“Handkerchiefs or aprons” — a tentmaker's working cloths in the city of the curious arts.

pos: n. pl. (the armpits; the hollow under the arm)
etymology: A plain English compound of arm and hole, used in 1611 for the armpit. The Hebrew 'atsiyl names the joint of the hand or the armpit.
biblical_def: Two passages use the word and they are exact opposites. Jeremiah had been let down with cords into the dungeon of Malchiah, where there was no water but mire, and he sank in the mire. Ebedmelech the Ethiopian went to the king, got thirty men, took old cast clouts and rotten rags from under the treasury, let them down by cords, and said: “Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so” (Jer 38:12). The rags were padding, so the cords would not cut the prophet as they drew him up. A foreign eunuch in a doomed city thought of the old man's armpits, and God took note of it: Ebedmelech is told by name that he shall not be given into the hand of the men he feared, because he had put his trust in the LORD. Ezekiel then has the counterfeit: “Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes, and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls!” (Eze 13:18). They too worked with cloth and armpits, and what they made was a cushion — comfort sewn for the arms of people God was calling to repent, and the prophet calls it hunting souls.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an armhole as the cavity under the shoulder, or armpit; also the hole in a garment for the arm.
webster_full: ARMHOLE, n. The cavity under the shoulder, or the armpit.
2. A hole for the arm in a garment.
Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes. Jer. xxxviii.
scriptures: And Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so.

And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes, and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls! Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive that come unto you?
For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel 13:18 names a ministry that specialises in comfort — pillows sewn to every armhole — and it is the exact description of preaching that will not disturb anyone.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 13 is a chapter against false prophets, and its second half is against women prophesying out of their own heart, whose particular trade is described in a startling figure: they sew pillows to all armholes and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature. The picture is of soft furnishing fitted to every size — a cushion for every arm, a veil for every head, comfort custom-made and universally available — and God calls it hunting souls. The charge is stated plainly in verse 22: with lies ye have made the heart of the righteous sad, whom I have not made sad; and strengthened the hands of the wicked, that he should not return from his wicked way, by promising him life. That is the mechanism of every comfortable ministry: it distresses the tender conscience by praising what God condemns, and it confirms the hardened one by promising life where God has promised none. Jeremiah 6:14 gives the same charge in one line — they have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace. Set against it stands Ebedmelech with his armful of rotten rags, giving real comfort to a real man in an actual pit, at real risk to himself. Scripture is not against padding. It is against padding sold in place of rescue.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'atsiyl (H679), the armpit, the joint of the arm; cechabah, cast clouts, rags; keceth (H3704), a pillow or cushion — the false prophetesses' work.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'atsiyl (H679) — the armpit, the arm-joint; used only in Jeremiah's rescue and Ezekiel's indictment; Jeremiah 38:12, Ezekiel 13:18.
Hebrew keceth (H3704) — a pad or cushion; the pillows sewn to hunt souls; Ezekiel 13:18, 13:20.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to lean upon with confidence; the reason given for Ebedmelech's deliverance; Jeremiah 39:18, Proverbs 3:5.
usage: “Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes” — padding for the cords that lifted a prophet from the mire.
“Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes” — comfort made to measure, and called hunting souls.
“Because thou hast put thy trust in me” — the LORD's word to an Ethiopian eunuch by name.

pos: n. (an awl; a pointed tool for boring; the instrument of the bondservant's permanent covenant)
etymology: Old English æl, an awl; the Authorized Version's spelling aul is the older form. The Hebrew martsea' is a boring tool, from a root meaning to pierce.
biblical_def: The law of the Hebrew servant runs six years, and in the seventh he goes out free for nothing. But there is a provision for the man who does not want to go: “if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free: then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever” (Exo 21:5-6). Deuteronomy repeats it: “thou shalt take an aul, and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise” (Deu 15:17). Every element preaches. The servant is legally free; the bondage that follows is chosen, and chosen for love, and the reason is stated aloud before witnesses. The ear is pierced — the organ of hearing and obedience — at the doorpost of the house he is entering for life. And the mark is permanent and visible. Psalm 40:6, quoted of Christ in Hebrews 10:5, says mine ears hast thou opened, literally digged; the Servant who said Lo, I come to do thy will, O God, came under this law voluntarily and for love.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an awl as a pointed instrument for piercing small holes in leather, used by shoemakers, saddlers and other workers in leather.
webster_full: AWL, n. A pointed instrument for piercing small holes in leather.
It is used by shoemakers, saddlers and other workers in leather.
His master shall bore his ear through with an aul. Ex. xxi.
scriptures: Exo 21:6
Then his master shall bring him unto the judges; he shall also bring him to the door, or unto the door post; and his master shall bore his ear through with an aul; and he shall serve him for ever.
Then thou shalt take an aul, and thrust it through his ear unto the door, and he shall be thy servant for ever. And also unto thy maidservant thou shalt do likewise.
Psa 40:8
I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.
corruption_summary: Freedom is now defined as the absence of binding commitments, so that a permanent, chosen, unbreakable servitude entered for love is unintelligible — which is precisely the shape of Christian discipleship and of marriage.
corruption_paragraphs: The bored ear is a scandal to the modern definition of liberty. Our culture defines freedom negatively, as the widest available range of open options, so that every permanent commitment is understood as a subtraction from a man's freedom and every irrevocable one as a kind of self-harm. Exodus 21 describes a man who has just been handed exactly that kind of freedom — the seventh year, out for nothing, no obligation — and who declines it, in public, before judges, because he loves his master and his wife and his children. He then accepts a mark he can never remove. Scripture treats this not as a tragedy but as the highest use a man can make of his liberty, and it is the New Testament's standing self-description for the Christian: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ; ye are not your own, for ye are bought with a price; his servants ye are to whom ye obey. The same logic governs the marriage vow, which is a binding of the will against the future preferences of the will, and church membership, and ordination. A generation taught to keep its options open finds all four incomprehensible and enters none of them wholeheartedly. Christ Himself is the archetype: mine ears hast thou opened; then said I, Lo, I come: I delight to do thy will, O my God.
roots_summary: Hebrew martsea' (H4836), an awl, a boring tool; karah (H3738), to dig or pierce, of Psalm 40:6; 'ebed 'owlam, a servant for ever.
roots_lines: Hebrew martsea' (H4836) — an awl; used only in the two statements of the bondservant law; Exodus 21:6, Deuteronomy 15:17.
Hebrew karah (H3738) — to dig, to open, to pierce; mine ears hast thou opened, applied to Christ in Hebrews 10:5; Psalm 40:6.
Hebrew 'ebed (H5650) — a servant, a bondman; the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah, and the title Paul takes for himself; Isaiah 42:1, Romans 1:1.
usage: “His master shall bore his ear through with an aul” — a permanent mark on a man legally free.
“Thrust it through his ear unto the door” — the ear, at the doorpost of the house he chose.
“I delight to do thy will, O my God” — the Servant who came under this law for love.

pos: n. (a signal-post on a height; a mast or pole set up alone as a mark)
etymology: Old English beacen, a sign or portent. In Isaiah 30 the beacon is not a fire but a bare pole left standing on a mountain — the one thing remaining after everything around it has fled.
biblical_def: Isaiah is rebuking Judah for trusting Egypt rather than the LORD, and he tells them what the alliance will buy: “One thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one; at the rebuke of five shall ye flee: till ye be left as a beacon upon the top of a mountain, and as an ensign on an hill” (Isa 30:17). The image is desolate. A people reduced until they are a single stripped mast on a summit — conspicuous, isolated, visible for miles, and a warning to everyone who sees it. And yet the very next verse turns: “And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you…blessed are all they that wait for him” (Isa 30:18). The same chapter that promises the beacon promises a Teacher who shall not be removed into a corner, and a voice behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it. Scripture does not leave the pole on the hill as the last word. The word also stands behind Mizpah — the heap of stones between Jacob and Laban, named as a watchtower where the LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a beacon as a signal erected on an eminence, consisting of a pitch barrel or combustibles to be fired at night, or of a pole set up as a mark; hence, that which gives notice of danger.
webster_full: BEACON, n. A signal erected on an eminence, consisting of a pitch barrel, or other combustible matter, to be fired at night, or upon the approach of an enemy, to alarm the country.
2. A mark or pole erected as a signal, or to give notice of danger.
3. Figuratively, that which gives notice of danger.
scriptures: One thousand shall flee at the rebuke of one; at the rebuke of five shall ye flee: till ye be left as a beacon upon the top of a mountain, and as an ensign on an hill.

And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you, and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you: for the LORD is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him.
And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
corruption_summary: A church stripped down to a lone pole on a hill is read as a failure, when Isaiah presents that condition as the point at which the LORD waits to be gracious.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A beacon is a signal on a height. The principle to recover is the shape of Isaiah 30, which runs from disaster to grace without an intervening improvement in the people. Judah is warned that her Egyptian alliance will end with a rout so complete that the survivors will be a single bare mast on a mountain top. Then verse 18: and therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you. Not nevertheless. The stripping is the occasion of the waiting. Churches and Christians in decline generally read their own reduction as evidence of God's displeasure or of their own irrelevance, and respond by reaching for a new alliance — a new method, a new partner, a new source of strength, which is exactly what Judah did in going down to Egypt. Isaiah names the alternative in verse 15, and Judah refused it: in returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not. The pole on the hill is not the end of the chapter. It is followed by a promise of teachers no longer removed into a corner and a voice behind saying, This is the way, walk ye in it — the guidance most audible to a man who has run out of alternatives.
roots_summary: Hebrew toren (H8650), a mast, a flagstaff, a pole; nec (H5251), an ensign or standard lifted up; mitspah (H4709), a watchtower, whence Mizpah.
roots_lines: Hebrew toren (H8650) — a mast or pole; the beacon left on the mountain, and the ship's mast of Ezekiel and Isaiah; Isaiah 30:17, 33:23.
Hebrew nec (H5251) — an ensign, a standard, a signal lifted up; the pole on which the brasen serpent was raised and the ensign for the nations; Numbers 21:8, Isaiah 11:10.
Hebrew mitspah (H4709) — a watchtower, a lookout; the heap between Jacob and Laban; Genesis 31:49.
usage: “Till ye be left as a beacon upon the top of a mountain” — a nation reduced to a bare pole.
“And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you” — the very next verse.
“Thine ears shall hear a word behind thee” — guidance most audible when the alternatives are gone.

pos: n. (a fishhook and line; the tackle of the individual fisherman, as distinct from the net and the drag)
etymology: Old English angul, a hook. To angle is to fish with hook and line; the Authorized Version keeps the noun, which modern English has almost entirely lost.
biblical_def: Isaiah, prophesying the drying up of the Nile, describes the ruin of a whole industry: “The fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish” (Isa 19:8). Three kinds of fisherman — hook, net, and those who work the waters generally — and all three out of work when the river fails. Habakkuk uses the same tackle for a far heavier charge. Complaining that God makes men as the fishes of the sea, he says of the oppressor: “They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad” (Hab 1:15) — and the next verse is the terrible one, therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat. A conqueror who worships his own instrument. That is the sin the whole prophecy is aimed at, and the answer given to Habakkuk is the great word Paul would quote three times: the just shall live by his faith. The New Testament then takes the tackle up in mercy: Peter is sent to cast an hook and take the fish with the tribute money in its mouth, and the fishermen of Galilee are made fishers of men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an angle as an instrument to take fish, consisting of a rod, a line and a hook; and to angle, to fish with such an instrument.
webster_full: ANGLE, n. An instrument to take fish, consisting of a rod, a line and a hook.
ANGLE, v.i. To fish with an angle, or with line and hook.
2. To fish for; to try to gain by some bait or insinuation; as, to angle for the hearts of men.
scriptures: Isa 19:8
The fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish.
Hab 1:15
They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad.
Hab 1:16
Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous.
corruption_summary: Habakkuk 1:16 names the most respectable idolatry there is — worshipping the instrument that made you prosperous — and it is the characteristic sin of successful men and successful ministries alike.
corruption_paragraphs: They sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous. It would be difficult to write a better description of what success does to a man. The Chaldean did not begin by worshipping his net; he began by using it, and it worked, and the working of it made him rich, and in time the tackle itself received the offerings. The idolatry is nearly invisible because the net is genuinely good and the prosperity is genuinely real. Every effective instrument is a candidate: a business method, a farming technique, an army, a political strategy, a church-growth model, a discipline of study, a translation of the Bible. Deuteronomy 8 warns Israel about it before they ever reach the land — lest thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth — and gives the corrective, thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth. The test is simple to state and painful to apply: what would happen in a man's soul if the net broke? Habakkuk asked how long God would tolerate the man burning incense to his drag, and the answer he was given was not an argument but a promise — the just shall live by his faith — and a vision of the day when the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.
roots_summary: Hebrew chakkah (H2443), a fishhook; cherem (H2764), a net; mikmereth (H4365), a fishing drag or seine.
roots_lines: Hebrew chakkah (H2443) — a fishhook, an angle; the tackle of Isaiah's mourning fishers and Habakkuk's conqueror; Isaiah 19:8, Habakkuk 1:15, Job 41:1.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a net; also, from the same root, a thing devoted to destruction, the ban; Habakkuk 1:15-16, Ecclesiastes 7:26.
Greek agkistron (G44) — a fishhook; used once, when Peter is sent to take the fish with the tribute money; Matthew 17:27.
usage: “All they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament” — an industry ruined when the river failed.
“They take up all of them with the angle” — men caught like fish by an empire.
“They sacrifice unto their net” — the idolatry of the instrument that made you rich.

pos: n. (a small vessel or case, especially a sealed flask of oil); also, the box tree of Lebanon
etymology: Latin buxus, the box tree, whose close-grained wood was used for small cases — hence the vessel took the tree's name. The Authorized Version uses both senses.
biblical_def: Elisha sent a young prophet on an errand with a sealed flask: “Gird up thy loins, and take this box of oil in thine hand, and go to Ramothgilead” (2Ki 9:1), and the instructions were exact: “Then take the box of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, Thus saith the LORD, I have anointed thee king over Israel. Then open the door, and flee, and tarry not” (2Ki 9:3). A whole dynasty fell out of that small vessel. The other sense is a tree: “I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” (Isa 41:19) — seven trees planted in a desert, that they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this. And again in the promise to Zion: “the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). The New Testament's alabaster box belongs to the same family of small vessels: a woman broke it over the Lord's head, and He said, she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a box as a case or vessel of wood, metal or other material, of various sizes; and separately the box tree, an evergreen of hard close-grained wood.
webster_full: BOX, n. A coffer or chest, either of wood or metal; in general, a case of any size and of any material.
2. A certain quantity or weight; as a box of sugar.
BOX, n. A tree or shrub, evergreen, of the genus Buxus, of very hard, close-grained wood, used by engravers.
scriptures: Then take the box of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, Thus saith the LORD, I have anointed thee king over Israel. Then open the door, and flee, and tarry not.
I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together:
The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.
corruption_summary: Great turning points in Scripture repeatedly hang on small vessels and unnamed messengers, against a habit of mind that measures a work of God by its scale.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A box is a box. What deserves notice is the recurring biblical pattern the box of oil belongs to. A young man whose name is never given carries a small flask to a military camp, pours it out, says nineteen words, and runs — and the house of Ahab is finished, Jezebel goes out of a window, and the Baal temple becomes a draught house. Elisha does not go himself. There is no ceremony, no crowd, and no follow-up. Scripture is full of this: a boy's five loaves; a widow's two mites, which the Lord said was more than all the rest; a little maid taken captive out of the land of Israel, whose one sentence sent Naaman to the Jordan; an alabaster box broken over a head, of which He said, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, there shall also this, that this woman hath done, be told for a memorial of her. The habit of measuring a work of God by its visible scale is not a modern invention, but modern instruments make it far easier to indulge, since everything is now counted. God has never worked that way, and the standing rule is Zechariah 4:10: for who hath despised the day of small things?
roots_summary: Hebrew pak (H6378), a small flask or vial of oil; te'ashshur (H8391), the box tree; Greek alabastron (G211), an alabaster flask.
roots_lines: Hebrew pak (H6378) — a small vial or flask; the box of oil for Jehu, and the vial Samuel poured on Saul; 2 Kings 9:1, 1 Samuel 10:1.
Hebrew te'ashshur (H8391) — the box tree; among the seven trees planted in the desert and the timber to beautify the sanctuary; Isaiah 41:19, 60:13.
Greek alabastron (G211) — an alabaster flask, sealed and broken to be used; the woman's offering at Bethany; Mark 14:3, Matthew 26:7.
usage: “Take this box of oil in thine hand, and go to Ramothgilead” — a dynasty ended out of a small flask.
“The fir tree, and the pine, and the box tree together” — seven trees planted in a desert.
“To beautify the place of my sanctuary” — the same timber brought to Zion.

pos: adj. (embroidered; worked with the needle in coloured thread; of the priest's coat and of the raiment God gave Jerusalem)
etymology: An older form of embroidered, from Old French brosder, to work with a needle. The Authorized Version distinguishes broidered work from the cunning work of the weaver.
biblical_def: The priest's wardrobe is listed in Exodus and the broidered coat is in it: “these are the garments which they shall make; a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe, and a broidered coat, a mitre, and a girdle: and they shall make holy garments for Aaron thy brother, and his sons…for glory and for beauty” (Exo 28:4). Then Ezekiel takes the same word for the most tender passage in his book. Jerusalem is drawn as a foundling cast out in the open field, unwashed and unswaddled, and the LORD passes by and says Live: “I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk” (Eze 16:10); “thou wast decked with gold and silver…and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom” (Eze 16:13). And then the turn, in the same chapter and the same vocabulary: “thou tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them: and thou hast set mine oil and mine incense before them” (Eze 16:18) — the very clothes He had given her, used to dress the idols. That is the anatomy of ingratitude in one word repeated three times.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to broider as to adorn with figures of needlework; to embroider — a word retained from the older English of the Scriptures.
webster_full: BROIDER, v.t. To adorn with figures of needle-work.
A robe, a broidered coat, and a girdle. Ex. xxviii.
BROIDERED, pp. Adorned with figures of embroidery.
scriptures: Exo 28:4

And these are the garments which they shall make; a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe, and a broidered coat, a mitre, and a girdle: and they shall make holy garments for Aaron thy brother, and his sons, that he may minister unto me in the priest's office.
I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers' skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk.
And tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them: and thou hast set mine oil and mine incense before them.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel 16 shows a soul using God's own gifts to dress its idols, which is the exact mechanism by which prosperity, gifting, and even ministry become the rivals of the God who gave them.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 16 is not primarily a chapter about a nation's wickedness; it is a chapter about the direction of gifts. Verse by verse God recites what He gave: life to a cast-out infant, washing, anointing, broidered work, badgers' skin for shoes, fine linen, silk, bracelets, a chain, a jewel on the forehead, a crown. Then verse by verse He recites where it all went: the garments to the high places, the jewels into images of men, His oil and His incense set before them, His meat, His fine flour, His honey, laid before them for a sweet savour. Nothing was thrown away. Everything was redirected. That is the ordinary form of idolatry among people who have been generously treated by God, and it is far more common than the worship of a carved figure. A man's gifting, given by God, is spent building his own name. A household's prosperity, given by God, is spent on a manner of life that has no room left for God. Even ministry itself, given by God, becomes the thing served. James 4:3 names the mechanism in the matter of prayer — ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts. The remedy is not to refuse the gifts, which God plainly delights to give, but to keep asking whose oil and whose incense is being set before what.
roots_summary: Hebrew tashbets (H8665), a checkered or broidered work, of the priest's coat; riqmah (H7553), embroidery, variegated needlework; roqem, the embroiderer, distinguished from the cunning workman.
roots_lines: Hebrew tashbets (H8665) — checkered or woven work; the broidered coat of the priest's garments; Exodus 28:4.
Hebrew riqmah (H7553) — embroidery, variegated work; the raiment God gave Jerusalem, and the eagle's divers colours in Ezekiel's parable; Ezekiel 16:10, 17:3.
Hebrew roqem (H7551) — the embroiderer, one who works with the needle; distinguished from the chosheb, the cunning weaver of the veil; Exodus 26:36, 26:31.
usage: “A robe, and a broidered coat, a mitre, and a girdle” — holy garments for glory and for beauty.
“I clothed thee also with broidered work” — the foundling given the raiment of a queen.
“Tookest thy broidered garments, and coveredst them” — His gifts dressing her idols.

pos: n. pl. (pieces of woven fabric; in Exodus, the “cloths of service” made for ministry in the holy place)
etymology: Old English clath. The Authorized Version distinguishes cloths, pieces of fabric, from clothes, garments worn — a distinction modern printing often blurs.
biblical_def: The phrase is fixed and it is repeated four times, which in Exodus means it matters: “the cloths of service, and the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons, to minister in the priest's office” (Exo 31:10; and again Exo 35:19, 39:1, 39:41). The material is named: “of the blue, and purple, and scarlet, they made cloths of service, to do service in the holy place” (Exo 39:1). These were not the priest's vestments — those are listed separately in the same breath — but the coverings and wrappings used in the work: the cloths in which the ark, the table, the candlestick, and the altar were wrapped when the camp moved, described in Numbers 4 with the same care. Somebody wove blue, purple, and scarlet for objects that would spend their travelling life inside a covering of badgers' skins where no Israelite would ever see them. The principle is stated in the phrase itself: cloths of service. Their whole purpose was the work, and their beauty was for God's eyes. Much of the labour of the tabernacle was of this kind, and much of the labour of the church still is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cloth as a manufacture or stuff of wool or hair, or of cotton, flax, hemp or other vegetable filaments, formed by weaving; and cloths as the plural, pieces of such stuff.
webster_full: CLOTH, n. A manufacture or stuff of wool or hair, or of cotton, flax, hemp or other vegetable filaments, formed by weaving or intertexture of threads.
2. The covering of a table; usually called table-cloth.
CLOTHS, plu. Pieces of cloth; distinguished from clothes, garments.
scriptures: And the cloths of service, and the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons, to minister in the priest's office,
The cloths of service to do service in the holy place, and the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and his sons' garments, to minister in the priest's office.
Num 4:6
And shall put thereon the covering of badgers' skins, and shall spread over it a cloth wholly of blue, and shall put in the staves thereof.
corruption_summary: Work no one will ever see is now hard to justify, in a culture where the visible portion of a labour has become the only portion that is thought to count.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Cloths are cloths. The point worth pressing is what was done with them. Blue, purple, and scarlet were the costliest dyes in the ancient world; the cloths of service were made of them; and much of that work went straight underneath a covering of badgers' skins to be carried through a wilderness. The congregation saw an ungainly bundle on the shoulders of the Kohathites. God saw blue. Scripture repeatedly commends labour done where only God is watching, and it is the plainest test of whether a work is being done for Him: alms in secret, prayer in the closet with the door shut, fasting with a washed face, and the Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. A culture organised around visibility finds this nearly impossible to value. Work that cannot be shown is assumed not to have happened; effort that produces no visible artefact is treated as waste; and the temptation in every ministry is to move resources toward the parts of the work that can be seen. The cloths of service are the corrective, and so is Colossians 3:23 — whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
roots_summary: Hebrew beged (H899), a garment or covering; bigdey hasserad, the cloths of service; tekeleth (H8504), blue, the costliest of the tabernacle dyes.
roots_lines: Hebrew beged (H899) — a garment, a covering, a cloth; the general word for the tabernacle textiles and for clothing; Exodus 31:10, Numbers 4:6.
Hebrew serad (H8278) — plaited or service work; the phrase bigdey hasserad, cloths of service, unique to these four verses; Exodus 31:10, 35:19, 39:1, 39:41.
Hebrew tekeleth (H8504) — blue, a costly dye; the cloth wholly of blue spread over the ark for its journey; Numbers 4:6, Exodus 26:1.
usage: “The cloths of service…to minister in the priest's office” — the phrase repeated four times in Exodus.
“Of the blue, and purple, and scarlet, they made cloths of service” — the costliest dyes for the unseen work.
“A cloth wholly of blue” — under the badgers' skins, where only God would see it.

pos: n. (a cord or ribbon used to fasten; in Exodus, the blue cord that bound the breastplate to the ephod and the plate to the mitre)
etymology: Old French laz, from Latin laqueus, a noose or cord. In the Authorized Version it never means the openwork fabric; it means a tie.
biblical_def: Two fastenings in the high priest's dress are made with a lace of blue, and each carries a doctrine. First the breastplate: “they shall bind the breastplate by the rings thereof unto the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, that it may be above the curious girdle of the ephod, and that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod” (Exo 28:28), and the workmen did exactly so (Exo 39:21). The breastplate carried the twelve names of the children of Israel, graven as signets, over Aaron's heart; the point of the blue lace was that it could not come loose. Aaron bore their names upon his heart before the LORD continually, and the fastening was specified so that it would never slip. Second the mitre: the plate of pure gold engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD was tied “on a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre; upon the forefront of the mitre it shall be” (Exo 28:37; Exo 39:31). The names over the heart, holiness on the forehead, both secured with the same blue cord. Hebrews says of the great High Priest that He ever liveth to make intercession for them, and the security of the fastening is the picture: those names do not come off.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lace as a string; a cord; a small cord used for fastening garments; and in later use, a work composed of threads interwoven into a net.
webster_full: LACE, n. A work composed of threads interwoven into a net, and worked on a pillow with spindles or pins.
2. A string; a cord; a small cord used for fastening or drawing together the parts of a garment.
Thou shalt put it on a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre. Ex. xxviii.
scriptures: And they shall bind the breastplate by the rings thereof unto the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, that it may be above the curious girdle of the ephod, and that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod.
And thou shalt put it on a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre; upon the forefront of the mitre it shall be.
And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goeth in unto the holy place, for a memorial before the LORD continually.
corruption_summary: Assurance is widely treated as a matter of how firmly the believer holds on, when the fastening Scripture describes was specified precisely so that the names could not come loose.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 28:28 gives a reason for a piece of cord, and the reason is the doctrine: that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod. Twelve names were cut into stones and worn over the high priest's heart every time he went into the holy place, and the LORD did not leave the attachment to the workman's judgment. He specified rings, and a blue lace, and a purpose — that it come not loose. Perseverance of the saints is that verse in doctrinal form, and it is a doctrine about God's grip rather than about the believer's. Christ says of His sheep, I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand; and Paul asks who shall separate us and works through the whole list — tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword, death, life, angels, principalities, powers, things present, things to come, height, depth, any other creature — and finds nothing on it. Two errors flank the truth. The first is a bare eternal security detached from perseverance, which tells a man who shows no fruit that a past decision has him fastened; the 1689 Confession is careful here, and holds that the saints will persevere, not merely that they cannot be lost. The second is the anxious religion that makes assurance depend on the strength of one's own grip, and so guarantees that the strongest believer will be the least troubled and the tenderest conscience the most tormented. The blue lace answers both. The fastening was God's work, it was specified, and its purpose was that the names should never be loosed.
roots_summary: Hebrew pathiyl (H6616), a cord, a thread, a lace; tekeleth (H8504), blue; choshen (H2833), the breastplate of judgment.
roots_lines: Hebrew pathiyl (H6616) — a twisted cord or thread; the blue lace of the breastplate and mitre, and the cord of Judah's signet; Exodus 28:28, 28:37, Genesis 38:18.
Hebrew choshen (H2833) — the breastplate of judgment, bearing twelve engraved stones; Exodus 28:15, 28:29.
Hebrew tsiyts (H6731) — the plate or flower of pure gold on the mitre, engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD; Exodus 28:36, 39:30.
usage: “That the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod” — a cord specified so the names could not slip.
“Thou shalt put it on a blue lace” — holiness fastened to the forefront of the mitre.
“Upon his heart…for a memorial before the LORD continually” — what the lace was holding.

pos: n. (an instrument for opening a lock; in Scripture, a figure of authority to admit and exclude)
etymology: Old English cæg. Ancient keys were large wooden or metal bars carried on the shoulder, which is why Isaiah can speak of laying the key upon a shoulder.
biblical_def: The word's first appearance is almost comic: Ehud has killed Eglon and locked the parlour behind him, and the servants “tarried till they were ashamed…therefore they took a key, and opened them: and, behold, their lord was fallen down dead on the earth” (Jdg 3:25). Then it becomes a figure of office. Shebna the steward is deposed and Eliakim installed: “the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isa 22:22) — the key of a great house was carried on the shoulder, and the man who bore it controlled all access. That verse is quoted by the risen Christ of Himself: “These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth” (Rev 3:7), and He tells Philadelphia, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it. Against these He sets a theft: “Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered” (Luk 11:52). Christ holds the keys; men can steal one and lock a door they cannot open.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a key as an instrument for shutting or opening a lock, by pushing the bolt one way or the other; and figuratively, that which serves to explain or to give entrance.
webster_full: KEY, n. An instrument for shutting or opening a lock, by pushing the bolt one way or the other.
2. An instrument by which something is screwed or turned.
3. That which serves to explain a cipher, or any thing difficult to be understood; also, a means of gaining or preventing entrance.
scriptures: And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.
Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
Rev 3:7

And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write; These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth;
corruption_summary: The keys of the kingdom have been claimed as a personal possession by an office in Rome, and the same theft Christ charged against the lawyers — taking away the key of knowledge — recurs wherever access to God is mediated by a class.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 16:19 gives the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and everything turns on what the keys are and who holds them. The Roman construction reads the promise as the personal endowment of one man and his successors, with the power of the keys exercised through a sacramental and jurisdictional system in which access to God is administered by a priesthood. The Reformed reading, which the dictionary holds, notes three things in the text and its context. First, Christ Himself is said in Revelation 3:7 to hold the key of David, quoting Isaiah 22:22 — the authority is His, and is exercised through His word. Second, the same binding and loosing is given to the whole assembly two chapters later in Matthew 18:18, in the context of church discipline, which is where the Confession locates it. Third, the keys are exercised by preaching: the gospel opens and shuts as it is proclaimed and received or refused, which is why Christ's complaint in Luke 11:52 is that the lawyers took away the key of knowledge. That is the recurring corruption in every tradition, not only Rome: a class that stands between the people and the Scriptures, entering not in themselves, and hindering them that were entering in. The Reformation answer was to hand the key back — an open Bible, in the common tongue, preached plainly — and Philadelphia's comfort still stands: I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it.
roots_summary: Hebrew maphteach (H4668), a key, an opener; Greek kleis (G2807), a key; Greek kleio (G2808), to shut.
roots_lines: Hebrew maphteach (H4668) — a key, from pathach, to open; the key of Eglon's parlour and the key of the house of David; Judges 3:25, Isaiah 22:22.
Greek kleis (G2807) — a key; the keys of the kingdom, the key of knowledge, and the keys of hell and of death which Christ holds; Matthew 16:19, Luke 11:52, Revelation 1:18.
Greek kleio (G2808) — to shut, to lock; he that openeth and no man shutteth; Revelation 3:7-8.
usage: “The key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder” — the steward's office, carried in the open.
“Ye have taken away the key of knowledge” — a key stolen and a door locked.
“He that openeth, and no man shutteth” — Christ claiming Isaiah's key as His own.

pos: v. (to join or bind closely together; used of hearts, of an army, and of the body of Christ)
etymology: Old English cnyttan, to tie in a knot. The Authorized Version uses it for the closest kind of joining short of becoming one flesh.
biblical_def: Israel gathered against Gibeah were “knit together as one man” (Jdg 20:11) — a nation bound into a single body for a single purpose. When David had finished speaking to Saul, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1Sa 18:1), and the covenant that followed cost Jonathan his robe, his garments, his sword, his bow, his girdle, and eventually his father's favour and his claim to a throne. David tests the men who come to him at Ziklag with the same word: “If ye be come peaceably unto me to help me, mine heart shall be knit unto you: but if ye be come to betray me to mine enemies…the God of our fathers look thereon, and rebuke it” (1Ch 12:17). Peter's sheet at Joppa was “a great sheet knit at the four corners” (Act 10:11). Paul then takes the word for the church: hearts comforted, being knit together in love (Col 2:2), and the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth. Knitting in Scripture is neither sentiment nor administration; it is the costly binding of one soul to another under covenant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to knit as to unite, as threads by needles; to join; to unite closely; to tie together; and figuratively, to unite firmly in affection.
webster_full: KNIT, v.t. To unite, as threads by needles; to connect in a kind of net-work.
2. To unite closely; as, to knit the bones.
3. To join or cause to unite; as, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David.
scriptures: So all the men of Israel were gathered against the city, knit together as one man.
And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Col 2:2

That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ;
corruption_summary: The friendship of David and Jonathan is now regularly recast as a romance, which requires ignoring both the text's own account of it and the covenant it was actually about.
corruption_paragraphs: A popular reading of 1 Samuel 18 and 2 Samuel 1 takes the knitting of souls and David's lament — thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women — as evidence of a sexual relationship, and the reading has moved from the academic margins into general circulation. It cannot be sustained from the text. The narrative is explicit about what the bond consisted of: Jonathan made a covenant with David (1Sa 18:3), stripped himself of his robe, his garments, his sword, his bow and his girdle, and gave them to David — the heir apparent handing over the insignia of succession to the man God had anointed in his place. Everything Jonathan does afterwards is of that kind: he pleads David's cause to Saul, warns him, and says in the wood at Ziph, Thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee. The love passing the love of women is loyalty in the face of dynastic self-interest, which is precisely the kind of love that women, in the marriages of that court, could not be expected to give. The corruption is not merely an error about two men; it is the reduction of every strong love to the erotic, and its cost is heaviest on friendship, which the modern world has almost no vocabulary left to describe. Scripture ranks covenant friendship very high: there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother, and greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
roots_summary: Hebrew qashar (H7194), to bind, to tie, to knit together; chaber (H2266), to join, to be coupled; Greek sumbibazo (G4822), to knit or compact together.
roots_lines: Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to bind or tie; the soul of Jonathan knit to David, and Jacob's life bound up in the lad's life; 1 Samuel 18:1, Genesis 44:30.
Hebrew chaber (H2266) — to join, to couple, to be in league; Jerusalem compact together, and the curtains of the tabernacle coupled; Psalm 122:3, Exodus 26:3.
Greek sumbibazo (G4822) — to knit or weld together, to compact; the church knit together in love and the body compacted by every joint; Colossians 2:2, Ephesians 4:16.
usage: “Knit together as one man” — a nation bound for a single purpose.
“The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David” — and a covenant, a robe, and a sword followed.
“Being knit together in love” — the apostolic prayer for the church.

pos: v. and adj. (loaded; burdened; the archaic past participle of lade)
etymology: Old English hladan, to load. The Authorized Version uses the strong participle laden where modern English says loaded, and Scripture loads three very different things.
biblical_def: First, a load of kindness: Joseph “sent after this manner; ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt, and ten she asses laden with corn and bread and meat for his father by the way” (Gen 45:23), sent by a brother whom the brothers had sold. Then a load of provision on an errand: “Jesse took an ass laden with bread, and a bottle of wine, and a kid, and sent them by David his son unto Saul” (1Sa 16:20) — a shepherd boy carrying a hamper to the king he would replace. Then a load of guilt: “Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters” (Isa 1:4). And finally the invitation that answers the third: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28). The Greek there is a perfect passive participle — those who have been loaded, and are still carrying it — and the verse is addressed not to the notoriously wicked but to people bent under a religion of works, since the chapter's next line offers a yoke that is easy and a burden that is light. Christ does not offer to remove all burdens. He offers to exchange the load.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines laden as the participle passive of lade: loaded; charged with a burden or freight; oppressed.
webster_full: LADEN, pp. of lade. Loaded; charged with a burden or freight.
LADE, v.t. To load; to put on or in, as a burden or freight.
Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden. Matt. xi.
scriptures: And to his father he sent after this manner; ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt, and ten she asses laden with corn and bread and meat for his father by the way.
Isa 1:4

Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters: they have forsaken the LORD, they have provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger, they are gone away backward.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: Matthew 11:28 is read as a general offer of relief from a busy life, when its context makes it an offer of relief from a religion of works — and the rest promised is a yoke.
corruption_paragraphs: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden is quoted more often than almost any verse in the Gospels, and usually with a modern load in mind: overwork, exhaustion, an over-full calendar, the general strain of contemporary life. Christ's hearers were carrying something else. The chapter has just pronounced woe on the cities that saw His mighty works and did not repent, and thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent; the burden in view is the one Matthew 23:4 describes, laid on men's shoulders by the scribes and Pharisees — heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, which they themselves would not move with one of their fingers. That is a religion of merit, and it is the specific weight the invitation lifts. The proof is in what follows immediately, which is very rarely quoted with it: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light. He does not promise an unyoked life. He promises a different yoke, worn with Him, from a Master who is meek and lowly — and the rest offered is rest unto the soul, which is what a man loaded with iniquity most needs and least expects to be given for nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew nasa' (H5375), to lift, to bear, to carry; kabed (H3513), to be heavy, weighty; Greek phortizo (G5412), to load, to burden.
