roots_lines: Hebrew nasa' (H5375) — to lift up, bear, carry away; used both of bearing a load and of bearing away sin; Genesis 45:23, Isaiah 53:12.
Hebrew kabed (H3513) — to be heavy, weighty, burdensome; the same root as kabod, glory, which is weight; Isaiah 1:4, Exodus 5:9.
Greek phortizo (G5412) — to load, to burden; the heavy laden whom Christ calls, and the burdens the lawyers laid on men; Matthew 11:28, Luke 11:46.
usage: “Ten asses laden with the good things of Egypt” — a load of kindness from a sold brother.
“A people laden with iniquity” — the load Isaiah names.
“All ye that labour and are heavy laden” — and the yoke offered in exchange.

pos: n. (a portion or plot of ground; a piece of land distinguished from the whole)
etymology: Old French parcelle, from Latin particula, a small part. In the Authorized Version it is almost always a parcel of ground, and the parcels it names are theologically weighted.
biblical_def: Jacob, coming to Shechem, “bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for an hundred pieces of money” (Gen 33:19) — a purchase in a land already promised to him, and he built an altar there. Centuries later: “the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought…and it became the inheritance of the children of Joseph” (Jos 24:32). Joseph had made the children of Israel swear it, by faith, on his deathbed in Egypt, and the promise was kept four hundred years later in a field his father had bought. Then Boaz at the gate: “Naomi, that is come again out of the country of Moab, selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech's” (Rut 4:3) — and the kinsman-redeemer must take the land and the widow together, which is the whole doctrine of redemption in a property transaction. And a parcel of barley: at Pasdammim “there was a parcel of ground full of barley; and the people fled from before the Philistines” (1Ch 11:13) — and Eleazar stood in the midst of it and defended it, and the LORD saved them by a great deliverance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a parcel as a portion of any thing taken separately; a part; a quantity or portion of land.
webster_full: PARCEL, n. A portion of any thing taken separately; a part, distinct from the rest.
2. A quantity or portion; as a parcel of land.
3. A part belonging to a whole; as, part and parcel.
scriptures: And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for an hundred pieces of money.

And the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for an hundred pieces of silver: and it became the inheritance of the children of Joseph.
Rut 4:3
And he said unto the kinsman, Naomi, that is come again out of the country of Moab, selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech's:
corruption_summary: God's promises are habitually expected on a timescale of weeks, and Scripture keeps its largest ones across centuries and through deathbed instructions that outlive the men who gave them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A parcel is a piece of ground. What the parcels teach is patience. Jacob bought a field at Shechem and pitched a tent on it. Joseph, dying in Egypt with a viceroy's honours, gave commandment concerning his bones — and Hebrews 11:22 lists that one act as the summary of his faith, not the coat, the dreams, the prison, or the throne. Four hundred years passed. A generation that had never seen Joseph carried a coffin out of Egypt, through the Red sea, forty years round a wilderness, over Jordan, and buried it at last in the field his father had bought, and the field became the inheritance of his children. There is no shortcut anywhere in that story. The habit of expecting God's promises on a short horizon is not new — the disciples asked, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel? — but a culture of immediate delivery makes it harder to resist, and it produces both premature despair and premature announcements. Hebrews 11 says of the patriarchs that these all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them. The bones went in the ground at Shechem because a man believed a promise he was told plainly he would not live to see.
roots_summary: Hebrew chelqah (H2513), a portion or parcel of ground; nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; ga'al (H1350), to redeem, of the kinsman's duty.
roots_lines: Hebrew chelqah (H2513) — a smooth piece of ground, a plot or parcel; Jacob's field at Shechem, Naboth's portion, and the barley field at Pasdammim; Genesis 33:19, 2 Kings 9:21, 1 Chronicles 11:13.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession by lot; what the parcel at Shechem became to Joseph's children; Joshua 24:32, Numbers 26:53.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman; the duty Boaz took up with the parcel and the widow together; Ruth 4:4-6, Leviticus 25:25.
usage: “He bought a parcel of a field…and built an altar” — a purchase in the land already promised.
“Buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought” — a promise kept four centuries later.
“Naomi…selleth a parcel of land” — redemption transacted at a city gate.

pos: n. pl. (a set of ranks or rows; a stand for cooking pots; in Kings, the ordered ranks of the temple guard)
etymology: Old French range, a row or rank. The Authorized Version uses it for two different Hebrew words: a cooking stand, and the drawn-up ranks of armed men.
biblical_def: The word first appears in the purity law: whatever a dead creeping thing falls upon is unclean, “whether it be oven, or ranges for pots, they shall be broken down: for they are unclean” (Lev 11:35) — the household fixtures themselves were to be demolished, not merely scoured. Then it names the ranks of the guard at the crowning of Joash. Athaliah had destroyed all the seed royal; one infant had been hidden six years in the house of God; and Jehoiada armed the captains and set them about the boy king: “ye shall compass the king round about, every man with his weapons in his hand: and he that cometh within the ranges, let him be slain: and be ye with the king as he goeth out and as he cometh in” (2Ki 11:8). When Athaliah came crying Treason, treason, the priest commanded, “Have her forth without the ranges: and him that followeth her kill with the sword. For the priest had said, Let her not be slain in the house of the LORD” (2Ki 11:15). Two details in that order deserve notice: the ranks were drawn to protect a child, and the house of the LORD was not to be defiled with blood even in the execution of a murderess.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a range as a row; a rank; things in a line; also a kitchen grate, and the extent or compass of a thing.
webster_full: RANGE, n. A row; a rank; things in a line; as a range of buildings; a range of mountains.
2. A class; an order.
3. A kitchen grate; a stand or grate for pots.
scriptures: And every thing whereupon any part of their carcase falleth shall be unclean; whether it be oven, or ranges for pots, they shall be broken down: for they are unclean, and shall be unclean unto you.
And ye shall compass the king round about, every man with his weapons in his hand: and he that cometh within the ranges, let him be slain: and be ye with the king as he goeth out and as he cometh in.

But Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains of the hundreds, the officers of the host, and said unto them, Have her forth without the ranges: and him that followeth her kill with the sword. For the priest had said, Let her not be slain in the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: The preservation of the messianic line ran, at one point, through a hidden infant and a ring of armed men, and Scripture treats the protection of the vulnerable as an ordered duty rather than a sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Kings 11 is one of the narrowest passes in redemptive history. Athaliah, daughter of Ahab, seized the throne of Judah and destroyed all the seed royal — a systematic massacre of the house of David, the line to which the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 was attached. One infant was stolen away by Jehosheba and hidden with his nurse in a bedchamber, then six years in the house of God. The whole promise of a son of David to sit upon his throne for ever hung, humanly speaking, on a woman's courage and a locked room. When the boy was brought out, Jehoiada did not trust to acclamation: he armed the captains, gave them the spears and shields that had been King David's, set them in ranks about the child, and gave a standing order — he that cometh within the ranges, let him be slain. Protection was organised, armed, and specific. Two things are worth drawing from it. The first is that God's preservation of His promises regularly runs through ordinary human faithfulness at great personal risk, and Jehosheba's name is in the record. The second is the shape of the duty: the ranks were drawn around a child who could not defend himself. Psalm 82:3-4 puts it as a command — defend the poor and fatherless; deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.
roots_summary: Hebrew kiyrayim (H3600), a pair of cooking stands, ranges for pots; sederah (H7713), a rank or row, of the temple guard; bayith (H1004), the house, which was not to be defiled with blood.
roots_lines: Hebrew kiyrayim (H3600) — a stand or range for pots; used only in the purity law of Leviticus 11:35.
Hebrew sederah (H7713) — a rank, a row, an ordered line; the armed ranks about the boy king; 2 Kings 11:8, 11:15.
Hebrew qesher (H7195) — a conspiracy, treason; Athaliah's cry when she saw the king by a pillar as the manner was; 2 Kings 11:14.
usage: “Whether it be oven, or ranges for pots, they shall be broken down” — the fixtures themselves demolished.
“He that cometh within the ranges, let him be slain” — a ring of armed men round a child.
“Let her not be slain in the house of the LORD” — even a just execution kept outside the sanctuary.

pos: n. pl. (torn and worn fragments of cloth; the clothing of poverty, and the material of an unlikely rescue)
etymology: Old Norse rögg, a tuft or shagginess. The Authorized Version uses rags for the end of a garment's life and, twice, for what such fragments are still good for.
biblical_def: Solomon gives the economic proverb: “the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21) — and note which of the three is named as the clothier. Drink and appetite bring poverty; it is drowsiness, the settled unwillingness to rise and work, that puts the rags on a man. The most memorable use is a scene of mercy. Jeremiah was sinking in the mire of Malchiah's dungeon when Ebedmelech “took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah” (Jer 38:11), telling him to put them under his armholes so the cords would not cut (Jer 38:12). The rescue was made out of the palace's discarded scraps — a rubbish heap under the treasury supplied what the treasury could not. And Isaiah 64:6 supplies the theological use, where all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags. Between them the word covers the whole range: rags as the wage of sloth, rags as the tenderness of a real rescue, and rags as the true valuation of our best works before God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rag as any piece of cloth torn from the rest; a tattered cloth, torn or worn till its texture is destroyed; and rags collectively, mean dress; tattered clothes.
webster_full: RAG, n. Any piece of cloth torn from the rest; a tattered cloth, torn or worn till its texture is destroyed.
2. Garments worn out; proverbially, mean dress.

corruption_summary: Two errors about poverty run side by side: one that treats every poor man as a sluggard, and one that denies that sloth impoverishes anybody — and Proverbs will not fund either.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs says that drowsiness clothes a man with rags, and it says it more than once: yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth. Paul is equally blunt: if any would not work, neither should he eat. That strand of Scripture is real and the church must not be embarrassed by it. But it is not the whole counsel, and using it as a general theory of poverty is a serious misuse. The same book says the destruction of the poor is their poverty, that the rich man's wealth is his strong city, and that he that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker. The law provided gleaning, the sabbath year, the jubilee, and a standing prohibition on taking a poor man's garment overnight — none of which would be necessary if every poor man were simply idle. Ecclesiastes observes that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, but time and chance happeneth to them all. Scripture therefore holds two things at once: sloth impoverishes, and poverty has many other causes, including oppression, disaster, illness, and providence. A church that preaches only the first becomes hard; a church that denies it becomes useless to the young man it should be warning. And over both stands Isaiah 64:6, which puts every man in the same clothes before God, and leaves nobody in a position to despise anybody.
